segments.description: Coaches, please join me in welcoming Simon Jones to the Virtual Grand Samp Coaches Conference. Following a professional playing career in tennis, during which time he competed at the Wimbledon Championships, Simon established a successful coaching business in Cardiff, Wales, where he was instrumental in guiding high-performance tennis players to national and world successes. An appointment as the national coach for the Lawn Tennis Association led to a 31-year career with a national governing body. During this time, Simon worked in a senior leadership role and increased the effectiveness of those coaching Britain's most talented athletes and also led great Britain teams to European and world titles. In 2022, Simon was appointed head of performance strategy at the Chelsea Football Club and this is his current role in addition to maintaining his consultancy support to elite sporting leaders. Today he sits down with Paul Aiken to talk through some of the lessons he has learnt on his incredible journey in tennis. Simon, you've worked at the pointy end in two sports for well over 30 years. Firstly in tennis, player development, coach development at the LTA and now soccer at Chelsea Football Club. What are some of the global trends that you're seeing in sport right now? I think the big thing, Paul, that we've got to think about is the way in which the world is changing for the young people that we're working with.

In my coaching in tennis and education and the coach development I do in football, we always looked at education. Education is really, of course it's relevant because we're educators. But one of the great expressions I heard from education is we cannot teach the youngsters of today like we were taught because that world does not exist anymore. And I think a lot of the work that we're doing at the Chelsea Academy is to think about what the modern learner is like and how that might influence the future of coaching. The sort of things I'm talking about is the world that a young person is in today is completely different to what it was like 20 years ago or when a lot of young people that are now coaches. And the research and the experts say that the next 10 years it's going to change exponentially at a speed that's never changed before. AI, chat, GPT, all of these things are changing the world around us. So I think really understanding the modern learner, understanding for example the prevalence of mental health issues with young people, understanding the massive influence that social media is having. So social media we used to say well we don't want them going on Twitter too much because we want them to interact with each other and of course we would say that but it's much way more than that. It's the way in which they can consume vast amounts of information and data through TikTok, through X, Twitter, all of the other channels

So, your 31-year career at the LTA heavily involved at the pointy end. Now, what are you seeing the difference between a, potentially, a soccer coach and a tennis coach? Yeah, well, there are obvious difference visually in the sports, of course. But there are many similarities that I noticed when I sort of crossed codes, as it were. The first one is that both sports are very traditional sports, hugely traditional sports. There are many, many sports that are less traditional, more modern sports. But tennis and soccer are two of the most traditional sports in the world. So, therefore, you've got this wisdom handed down by the elders of generations of information and ways of doing things. So, that is something to consider. The next thing is that the coaching workforce in the performance level in both sports often comes from the same place, which is ex-players. So, the challenges that ex-players have in getting their message across or learning really good pedagogical ways of coaching, those are the challenges that ex-players often have because they're coming with a superior knowledge of the game and understanding the competitive arenas. Those two things are the same in football and tennis. If I was working with 20 coaches, 10 of each, and they were not dressed in their uniforms, sometimes it would be hard to tell the difference. And then another aspect is that both sports at the performance end are all about next competition, very, very competition-based, very competition-based.
